title: Albaloo polo
subtitle: Persian sour cherry and saffron rice
excerpt: Albaloo polo is Persian rice cooked with sour morello cherries, saffron, and sugar until the fruit is jammy and the grains are stained a deep ruby. It is a celebration rice with a vivid sweet-sour flavour, served with braised chicken or on its own.
sourceNotes: Najmieh Batmanglij, Food of Life: Ancient Persian and Modern Iranian Cooking and Ceremonies (1986). Albaloo polo documented as a summer celebration rice from Tehran. Margaret Shaida, The Legendary Cuisine of Persia (1992). Notes on the use of morello cherries and the sweet-sour balance.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The cherry mixture can be made a day ahead. Cook the rice fresh on the day.

content.text: Albaloo polo is a Persian rice dish layered with sour cherries cooked with sugar into a glossy, jammy compote. The cherries stain the rice ruby and give a sweet-sour flavour that is unusual and striking. It is a summer dish when morello cherries are available, though jarred sour cherries (drained from syrup) work almost as well. The rice is cooked using the standard chelow method to form a tahdig crust.

items.prepNote: ground, dissolved in 3 tbsp hot water
morello or sour cherries, fresh or from a jar (drained)

content.text: If using fresh {{cherries}}, pit them. Place in a saucepan with {{caster-sugar}} and {{cinnamon-ground}} if using. Cook over a medium heat, stirring, for 10 to 15 minutes until the cherries have softened and the juice has thickened to a loose syrup. Taste: sour cherries need more sugar than sweet ones. Add {{unsalted-butter}} and stir to combine. Set aside.
Bring a large pot of water to the boil with {{sea-salt-fine}}. Add the rinsed {{basmati-rice}} and parboil for six to seven minutes until just tender outside but chalky within. Drain in a colander.

Heat {{sunflower-oil}} in a large heavy saucepan with 3 tablespoons of water. Spread a thin layer of parboiled rice over the base. Add a layer of cherry mixture, then a layer of rice, alternating until all the rice and cherries are used. End with a layer of rice.

Drizzle the dissolved {{saffron}} water over the top layer. Wrap the lid in a clean tea towel, cover the pan, and steam on medium-high for three minutes to build steam, then on the lowest heat for 30 to 35 minutes. The base should be a dark, caramelised tahdig.
Rest on a cold wet cloth for two minutes. Spoon the ruby-stained rice onto a platter and invert the tahdig on top. Serve immediately.

items.symptom: The cherries are too sharp even after adding sugar
items.cause: Morello cherries vary greatly in acidity
items.fix: Add sugar a tablespoon at a time, tasting between each addition. The cherry mixture should taste pleasantly sweet-sour, not puckering.

items.symptom: The rice is turning grey rather than ruby
items.cause: Cherry syrup not deep enough in colour
items.fix: Cook the cherries until the syrup is very concentrated and dark. The colour is what stains the rice.

items.symptom: The tahdig burned through the cherry syrup
items.cause: The sugary cherry mixture burns faster than plain oil
items.fix: Keep the base layer of rice plain (no cherry mixture touching the pan base) and layer the fruit only above this base.

items.symptom: The rice grains are sticking together in clumps
items.cause: Not rinsed well enough before parboiling
items.fix: Rinse until the water runs absolutely clear: this removes the surface starch that causes sticking.

content.text: Albaloo polo is a Tehran speciality, linked to the summer fruit season when small, sour morello cherries (albaloo) are sold at street stalls. Sweet-sour fruit combined with saffron rice is a classic Persian pairing, and fruit polo appears in many forms across the cuisine: barberry rice (zereshk polo), dried apricot rice, pomegranate rice. The cherry version is one of the most festive and is served at celebrations and family gatherings. Paired with braised chicken or lamb shoulder, it becomes a complete celebration meal.
